segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter had sworn he would die before he would ever deny Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, in one terrible night, he denied him three times. The rooster crowed, Jesus turned and looked at him, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the resurrection, Peter went back to fishing. Back to the old life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is what people do with a failure they cannot carry. They go back to what they knew before it happened. And that night they caught nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At dawn, a figure on the shore called out across the water to the boat.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Children, have ye any meat?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Have you caught anything, he called. And they had to say it out loud to a stranger — no. Nothing. All night, nothing.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Cast the net on the right side of the ship, and ye shall find.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Put the net over the right side, he told them, and you will find some. They did — and it came up so full they could not haul it in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of them went very still and said, it is the Lord. And Peter did not wait for the boat. He threw himself into the sea and swam for shore, leaving everything behind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he waded out of the water, he stopped cold. On the sand was a charcoal fire, with fish already laid over it, and bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A charcoal fire. The same kind of fire Peter had stood beside in the courtyard the night he denied him. The smell alone would have brought the whole night back.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus did not bring up the denial. He simply had breakfast waiting, and they ate together on the shore in the first gold light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When breakfast was over, Jesus turned to Peter. Three times, once it seems for each denial, he asked him the same question, using Peter's old name, the name he had before any of it:

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not, how could you. Not, prove it. Not one word thrown back at him about the denial. Only: do you love me.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three times Peter answered him, yes, Lord, you know that I love you. Each time it cost him more, and each time he meant it more.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Feed my sheep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Feed my sheep. To the man who had failed him worst, Jesus handed the biggest job of all. He did not only forgive Peter. He trusted him again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is how good he is. He takes your worst night and hands you back your life, with a purpose bigger than the one you thought you had thrown away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter went back to fishing because he thought his failure was final. Is there a failure you have quietly decided is final?
